problem: Novelty-based exploration bonuses such as RND (random visual features) and NGU (inverse-dynamics controllable states) define novelty in a visual feature space. In partially-observable 3D environments that space is noisy and not semantic: different viewpoints or colors of the same scene look novel, while semantically distinct states can look alike. Exploration is therefore narrow and sample-inefficient.
motivation: Good state abstractions for exploration are task-dependent. Learning them requires the very exploration they are supposed to drive, a chicken-and-egg problem. Natural language is inherently abstract: it groups causally similar situations, separates distinct ones, and omits irrelevant detail (a TV with static is just 'a TV with no signal'). So representations shaped by language, including vision-language models pretrained on image captions, should give a compact but sufficient novelty space without needing environment-specific annotation.
key_idea: Compute the intrinsic novelty reward (NGU episodic kNN novelty or RND-style distillation error) on frozen pretrained language-shaped embeddings (CLIP/ALM text embeddings of oracle captions, or CLIP/ALM image embeddings of the raw frame) instead of on learned or random visual features, while the policy itself is still trained from scratch on pixels.
insight: Language helps exploration for two separable reasons. It coarsens the state space: Lang-RND learns 'lift' 33% faster than Vis-RND and solves 'put' just as Vis-RND starts to learn. It also carves the space along semantic lines: LD beats S-LD, a control whose captions are a random, marginal-matched partition of visual random features; S-LD only helps on the easy 'lift' task and fails on 'put' and 'find'. The benefit comes from the captioning-pretraining knowledge rather than from representations simply being frozen: a frozen, pre-converged inverse-dynamics model (pretrained Vis-NGU) is no better, and possibly worse. The benefit also depends on rich language rather than pretraining per se: ImageNet NFNet embeddings help object-centric 'lift'/'put' but hurt the multi-object 'find' task. Image-only LSE embeddings nearly match oracle-caption embeddings in Playroom, so no language oracle is needed at test or train time.
method: Language oracle (analysis/Lang variants only): Unity-state-based captioner producing a scene description O_L (visible objects and interactions in Playroom; looked-at object in City). O_L is used only for the intrinsic reward and is never given to the policy.

Lang-NGU: simplified NGU episodic novelty (single beta, long-term modulator alpha=1; kNN L2 kernel over an episodic memory of 12,000). States are embedded by frozen pretrained text encoders (BERT, CLIP_text, Small/Med-ALM_text) applied to O_L.

LSE-NGU: the same episodic novelty, but on frozen CLIP_image or ALM_image embeddings (Language-Supervised Embeddings) of the RGB frame, so no oracle is needed. Embeddings are added to the buffer only every 8 steps, which was crucial and also saves inference cost; intrinsic reward is normalized in Playroom.

ND (network distillation): RND variant in which a small trainable CNN/MLP learns to regress the outputs of a frozen pretrained ALM encoder (Small-ALM image or text). The regression error is the lifetime-novelty reward.

Analysis variants: Lang-RND (RND on the caption with random targets), LD (reward = NLL of the oracle caption under a CNN-LSTM captioner trained online), and S-LD (captions from a fixed random smooth partition of visual random features, quantile-matched to LD's caption marginal).

Agent: ResNet image encoder + LSTM instruction encoder + LSTM memory with MLP policy/value heads, trained from scratch with IMPALA (Playroom, separate extrinsic/intrinsic value heads) or R2D2 (City). Reward is r_e + beta*r_i; 256 actors; exploration networks share no parameters with the policy.

setting.backbone: ResNet + LSTM policy trained from scratch with RL (IMPALA on Playroom, R2D2 on City); frozen CLIP / ALM (ALIGN-trained) / BERT encoders used only to compute the intrinsic reward during training
setting.model_size: policy small (ResNet channels 16/32/32, LSTM 256); reward encoders frozen: Small-ALM 25M ResNet image + 44M BERT text, Med-ALM 71M NFNet + 77M BERT, CLIP; ImageNet control 71M NFNet-F0
setting.training_data: Online RL in procedurally generated Unity environments (Playroom single-room lift/put, multi-room find; City pure exploration), 8-36 h on 2x2 TPUv2 with 256 actors. No extra data; pretrained encoders (CLIP, ALIGN-trained ALM) used frozen, not fine-tuned.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB 96x72 + language goal instruction (oracle captions used only for intrinsic reward in Lang-* variants, never by the policy)
setting.action_space: discrete: Playroom 46 actions (locomotion + object grasp/rotate); City 8 actions (move forward/back/left/right, look left/right, move-forward-and-look left/right); action repeat 4
setting.privileged: none at test time; during training, Lang-NGU/Lang-RND/LD/text-ND use Unity-state oracle captions for the intrinsic reward (LSE-NGU and image-ND do not)

numbers.backbone: R2D2 ResNet+LSTM policy; frozen Small-ALM image encoder for intrinsic reward
numbers.extra: No official split; a new map is procedurally generated each episode. Pure exploration with no extrinsic reward, 11,250-step episodes. Coverage = unique bins of a 32x32 grid (1024 bins, not all reachable), mean ± s.e. over 5 replicas.

numbers_note: Only the City coverage table (Table S3) gives exact numbers. All Playroom results (lift/put/find success curves, sample efficiency, object-interaction stats) appear only in figures; the text summarizes them as relative speed-ups (50-70% on lift/put, 18-38% on find, ND 41% faster on find, Lang-RND 33% faster on lift). This is an RL exploration paper in non-standard Unity environments, not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark.
results: In City pure exploration, Lang-NGU covers 241 bins (Small-ALM) and LSE-NGU 162 bins without any oracle, versus 83 for Vis-NGU (controllable state), 111 for ImageNet embeddings and 60 for random actions; that is roughly 3x and 2x the baseline, against 346 for a ground-truth-coordinate agent. In Playroom, Lang-NGU/LSE-NGU improve sample efficiency over Vis-NGU by 50-70% on lift/put and 18-38% on find, and ALM-ND learns find 41% faster than Vis-RND. Image-only LSE variants nearly match their oracle-caption counterparts.
limitations: Pretrained CLIP/ALM representations handle multi-object, cluttered scenes less well, so gains are smaller on the 'find' search task; transfer to visually non-naturalistic domains (e.g. Atari) is unclear.

Oracle-language variants rely on hand-built Unity captions that are less rich than human language. Evaluation is only in DeepMind-internal Unity environments (Playroom, City) with most results given as learning curves, not on standard navigation benchmarks.
Large frozen encoders add inference cost in distributed RL; this is mitigated by embedding only every 8 steps and by using Small-ALM in City.
